primary.key: And sometimes I do not reach, but fall to the ground midway. What then can be the use of going up ninety thousand li in order to start for the south?”
primary.s: Laughing at the great bird’s climb, a cicada tells a young dove of its own short hops; Guo Xiang, on chapter 1, reads it as each content in its own nature, the great not prizing itself, the small not envying, both equally at ease.
primary.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 1, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 1, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6351652 (2026)

basis.words: 苟足於其性，則雖大鵬無以自貴於小鳥，小鳥無羨於天池，而榮願有餘矣。故小大雖殊，逍遙一也。
basis.gloss: If each is satisfied in its own nature, then even the great Peng has nothing by which to prize itself above the small bird, and the small bird does not envy the Heavenly Pool, and both have honour and wishes to spare. So though small and great differ, their free and easy wandering is one.

standby.key: Thus it has been said, “The perfect man ignores self; the divine man ignores action; the true Sage ignores reputation.”
standby.s: After Lieh Tzŭ, who rides the wind yet still needs it, the chapter names three kinds of man; Guo Xiang, on chapter 1, reads having no self as following things, and having no merit as going along without helping, at one with the utmost principle.
standby.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 1, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 1, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6351652 (2026)

basis.words: 無己，故順物，順物而至矣。…今順而不助，與至理為一，故無功。
basis.gloss: [On the perfect man:] Having no self, he follows things; following things, he reaches the utmost. … [On the divine man:] Now he follows and does not help along, and is one with the utmost principle; therefore he has no merit.

primary.key: But what is it that gives to each the individuality, to all the potentiality, of sound?
primary.s: Asked what Heaven’s music is, beyond wind in hollows and human pipes, Tzŭ Ch’i answers with a question; Guo Xiang, on chapter 2, reads Heaven’s music as no separate thing but the hollows and pipes themselves, each sounding of itself, with no one rousing them.
primary.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 2, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 2, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 5978516 (2026)

basis.words: 夫天籟者，豈復別有一物哉？即眾竅比竹之屬，接乎有生之類，會而共成一天耳。…物皆自得之耳，誰主怒之使然哉。
basis.gloss: The piping of Heaven: is it some other thing besides? It is just the hollows, the bamboo pipes and their like, joined with all living kinds, meeting together to make up one Heaven. … Things all get it of themselves; who is the master that rouses them to be so?

standby.key: And when that axis passes through the centre at which all Infinities converge, positive and negative alike blend into an infinite ONE.
standby.s: Tzŭ Ch’i, discoursing on this and that, comes to where opposites lose their pairs; Guo Xiang, on chapter 2, reads the centre as the empty middle of the endless ring of right and wrong, where holding neither, one answers both without end.
standby.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 2, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 2, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 5978516 (2026)

basis.words: 夫是非反覆，相尋無窮，故謂之環。環中，空矣；今以是非為環而得其中者，無是無非也。無是無非，故能應夫是非。是非無窮，故應亦無窮。
basis.gloss: Right and wrong turn over and over, chasing each other without end; so it is called a ring. The middle of the ring is empty; one who takes right and wrong as the ring and gains its middle has neither right nor wrong. Having neither, he can answer right and wrong. Right and wrong are endless, so his answering too is endless.

primary.key: “How do I know that love of life is not a delusion after all? How do I know but that he who dreads to die is not as a child who has lost the way and cannot find his home?
primary.s: Answering Chü Ch’iao on the sage, Chang Wu Tzŭ turns to life and death; Guo Xiang, on chapter 2, reads life and death as one, so that delighting in life alone sets itself against change, and death may be the strayed child’s return home.
primary.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 2, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 3, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6364018 (2026)

basis.words: 死生一也，而獨悅生，欲與變化相背，故未知其非惑也。…少而失其故居，名為弱喪。夫弱喪者，遂安於所在而不知歸於故鄉也。焉知生之非夫弱喪，焉知死之非夫還歸而惡之哉。
basis.gloss: Death and life are one, yet to delight in life alone is to wish to turn one’s back on change; so one cannot know it is not a delusion. … To lose one’s old home when young is called being lost young. One lost young settles where he is and does not know to return to his home country. How can one know that life is not such a being lost young, or that death is not a returning home, which is hated all the same?

standby.key: The universe and I came into being together; and I, and everything therein, are ONE.
standby.s: Having called an autumn spikelet great and a mountain small, Tzŭ Ch’i goes further; Guo Xiang, on chapter 2, reads it as each being sufficient in its nature, so heaven and earth are no older than the self, nor the myriad things different.
standby.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 2, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 3, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6364018 (2026)

basis.words: 苟各足於其性，則秋豪不獨小其小而太山不獨大其大矣。…苟足於天然而安其性命，故雖天地未足為壽而與我並生，萬物未足為異而與我同得。
basis.gloss: If each is sufficient in its own nature, then the autumn hair is not alone in being small in its smallness, nor Mount Tai alone great in its greatness. … If one is sufficient in what is so of itself and at rest in one’s nature and lot, then heaven and earth are not enough to count as long-lived, and are born together with me; the myriad things are not enough to count as different, and attain together with me.

primary.key: Now I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly dreaming I am a man.
primary.s: Closing the chapter, Chuang Tzŭ tells of waking from a butterfly dream; Guo Xiang, on chapter 2, reads it as each state suiting its own moment, so the present hundred years cannot be told from a dream, and mourning death while alive is an error.
primary.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 2, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 3, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6364018 (2026)

basis.words: 然所在無不適志，則當生而係生者，又當死而戀死矣。由此觀之，知夫在生而哀死者誤也。…而各適一時之志，則無以明胡蝶之不夢為周矣。世有假寐，而夢經百年者，則無以明今之百年，非假寐之夢者也。
basis.gloss: Yet wherever he is, he is content; so one who, alive, clings to life would, dead, cling to death. Seen this way, one who while alive grieves over death is in error. … Each suits the mind of its own moment, so there is no making clear that the butterfly is not dreaming it is Zhou. There are those who nap and dream through a hundred years; so there is no making clear that the present hundred years is not a napper’s dream.

standby.key: My life has a limit, but my knowledge is without limit. To drive the limited in search of the limitless, is fatal; and the knowledge of those who do this is fatally lost.
standby.s: Before Prince Hui’s cook and his blade, the chapter opens with a warning; Guo Xiang, on chapter 3, reads limitless knowledge as the craving of those who prize fame and love to win, which a bounded nature cannot chase without exhaustion.
standby.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 3, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 4, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6353040 (2026)

basis.words: 夫舉重擔輕而神氣自若，此力之所限也。而尚名好勝者，雖復絕膂，猶未足以慷其願。此知之無涯也。…以有限之性尋無極之知，安得而不困哉。
basis.gloss: To lift the heavy and carry the light with the spirit composed: that is the limit of strength. But those who prize fame and love to win, though they break their backs, still cannot satisfy their wishes. This is knowledge without limit. … To seek limitless knowledge with a limited nature: how could one not be exhausted?

primary.key: Then the soul will be a negative existence, passively responsive to externals. In such a negative existence, only TAO can abide. And that negative state is the fasting of the heart.”
primary.s: Counselling Yen Hui before he goes to the headstrong Prince of Wei, Confucius explains a fast; Guo Xiang, on chapter 4, reads it as setting aside ears, eyes, mind and intent, trusting the breath’s own nature, for in an emptied heart the utmost Way gathers.
primary.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 4, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 5, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 7907034 (2026)

basis.words: 遺耳目，去心意，而付氣性之自得，此虛以待物者也…虛其心則至道集於懷也。
basis.gloss: [On the breath, empty and waiting on things:] Leave ears and eyes, drop mind and intent, and entrust all to the breath-nature attaining of itself: this is being empty and waiting on things. … [On the Way gathering in emptiness:] Empty the heart, and the utmost Way gathers in one’s bosom.

standby.key: But if he simply confines himself to his work, and is utterly oblivious of self, what leisure has he for loving life or hating death?
standby.s: Answering the Duke of Shê’s dread, Confucius speaks of a minister’s lot; Guo Xiang, on chapter 4, reads it as taking what comes and going straight ahead, for one whose trust in the Way wavers, planning for life and fearing death, never finishes his task.
standby.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 4, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 5, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 7907034 (2026)

basis.words: 理無不通，故當任所遇而直前耳。若乃信道不篤而悅惡存懷，不能與至當俱往而謀生慮死，未見能成其事者也。
basis.gloss: The pattern of things is nowhere blocked, so one should take whatever one meets and go straight ahead. If trust in the Way is not firm, and liking and loathing stay in the heart, one cannot go along with what is fitting but plans for life and worries over death; such a one has never been seen to complete his task.

primary.key: All men know the use of useful things; but they do not know the use of useless things.”
primary.s: Closing the chapter, the eccentric Chieh Yü, passing Confucius’ door, speaks of cinnamon and lacquer trees cut down for use; Guo Xiang, on chapter 4, reads it as the useful spending itself on another’s achievement while the useless keeps its own life whole.
primary.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 4, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 5, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 7907034 (2026)

basis.words: 有用則與彼為功，無用則自全其生。夫割肌膚以為天下者，天下之所知也。
basis.gloss: Being useful, a thing makes achievement for another; being useless, it keeps its own life whole. Those who cut their own flesh for the world’s sake, the world knows of.

standby.key: “A man,” replied Confucius, “does not seek to see himself in running water, but in still water. For only what is itself still can instil stillness into others.
standby.s: Asked by Ch’ang Chi why people make so much of Wang T’ai, Confucius answers; Guo Xiang, on chapter 5, reads it as still water that mirrors without stilling itself to mirror, just as crowds come to Wang T’ai of themselves, not drawn by him.
standby.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 5, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 6, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6353768 (2026)

basis.words: 夫止水之致鑒者，非為止以求鑑也。故王駘之聚眾，眾自歸之，豈引物使從己。
basis.gloss: Still water brings about a reflection, not by stilling itself in order to seek a reflection. So with Wang Tai’s gathering of followers: the followers come to him of themselves; how would he draw things to follow him?
